summary: Describes a way to keep network topology private when paths are computed across several domains by cooperating PCEs. Hidden segments of a path are replaced by an encrypted path key, so operators need not reveal their internal layout.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network operator asks another operator to help work out a route across both networks, the reply usually has to name the routers inside the other operator's network. This document offers a way around that: the second operator replies with a token instead of the real list of routers, and the token is only unlocked later, by the router at the edge that actually needs the detail.

questions: what is a path key in pce
how to keep topology confidential in inter-domain path computation
what is a confidential path segment
how does a pce hide topology between domains
subtitle: How a path computation element can hand back a locked token instead of its internal path, so cooperating networks keep their topology private.

tldr.problem: When several Path Computation Elements cooperate to compute a path across domains, returning the path segment inside another provider's network would reveal that network's internal topology.
tldr.mechanism: The PCE replaces the confidential part of the path with a Path-Key Subobject, a small token holding a path-key and the ID of the PCE that can decode it. The router that must continue signaling later sends that token back to the PCE to get the real hops.
tldr.outcome: Confidentiality is kept while the full path is still computed in one go, which avoids the path diversity problem that the earlier loose-hop technique had.

facts.label: Wait before a path-key is reused

today: RFC 5520 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating document, so it remains the way to keep a computed path segment confidential while still computing the whole path in one go.

sections.title: Why the Path Cannot Be Shared
sections.content:
Path computation using the Path Computation Element (PCE) is described in RFC 4655, and allows path computation of inter-domain Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Traffic Engineering and Generalized MPLS Label Switched Paths. An important element of inter-domain TE is that TE information is not shared between domains, for scalability and confidentiality reasons, so a single PCE is unlikely to be able to compute a full inter-domain path.

Cooperating PCEs can each compute the segment of the path across one domain. If confidentiality is required between domains, which would very likely be the case between Autonomous Systems belonging to different Service Providers, then cooperating PCEs cannot exchange path segments, or else the receiving PCE and the Path Computation Client will be able to see the individual hops through another domain. The part of the path that is to be kept confidential is called the Confidential Path Segment (CPS).

One way to preserve the confidentiality of the CPS is for the PCE to return a path containing a loose hop in place of the segment that must be kept confidential. The TE LSPs are then signaled as normal, and when a loose hop is encountered in the explicit route it is resolved by performing a secondary path computation at or on behalf of a Label Switching Router at a domain boundary. That technique has a serious drawback. The PCE-based computation model is particularly useful for finding mutually disjoint inter-domain paths, and with loose hops each TE LSP must be recomputed at the domain boundaries as it is signaled. Because the signaling proceeds independently for each LSP, disjoint paths cannot be guaranteed, since the routers that expand the explicit route objects are not synchronized. With loose hops, path segment confidentiality and path diversity are mutually incompatible.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators usually do not want to tell a competitor which routers sit between the border routers of their network. The usual way around that is to return a loose hop, a name that says only the destination, and let the receiving side work out the route later. The catch is that this loses the ability to guarantee two routes that do not share any link, because each route is worked out separately at the border.

sections.title: The Path-Key Solution
sections.content:
A PCE computes a path segment related to a particular domain and replaces any CPS in the path reported to the requesting PCC, or to another PCE, by one or more subobjects referred to as PKSes. The entry boundary LSR of each CPS SHOULD be specified using its TE Router Id as a hop in the returned path immediately preceding the CPS, and other subobjects MAY be included immediately before the hop identifying the boundary LSR to indicate link and label choices. The exit node of a CPS MAY be present as a strict hop immediately following the PKS.

During path computation, when local policy dictates that confidentiality must be preserved for all or part of the path segment being computed, or if explicitly requested by the path computation request, the PCE associates a path-key with the computed path for the CPS, places its own identifier, its PCE ID, along with the path-key in a PKS, and inserts the PKS object in the path returned to the requesting PCC or PCE immediately after the subobject that identifies, using the TE Router Id, the LSR that will expand the PKS into explicit path hops. This will usually be the LSR that is the starting point of the CPS.

The PCE that generates a PKS SHOULD store the computed path segment and the path-key for later retrieval. A local policy SHOULD determine for how long to retain that stored information, and whether to discard it after it has been queried. It is RECOMMENDED for a PCE to store the PKS for a period of 10 minutes.

A path-key value is scoped to the PCE that computed it, as identified by the PCE-ID carried in the PKS. A PCE MUST NOT re-use a path-key value to represent a new CPS for at least 30 minutes after discarding the previous use of the same path-key. A PCE that cannot retain information about previously used path-key values across a restart SHOULD use some other mechanism to guarantee uniqueness, such as embedding a timestamp or version number in the path-key. The term path-key here is an identifier allocated by a PCE to represent a segment of a computed path; it has no relation to a cryptographic key.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a loose hop, the PCE returns a token that stands for the hidden stretch of route. It keeps the real route in its own memory, together with the token, and remembers it for about ten minutes. A token is only good for one PCE, and the PCE must not hand out the same token again for at least half an hour after throwing it away, so that a stale token cannot silently mean a different route.

sections.title: Expanding a Path-Key
sections.content:
A head-end LSR that is a PCC converts the path returned by a PCE into an explicit route object (ERO) that it includes in the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Path message. If the path returned by the PCE contains a PKS, this is included in the ERO. Like any other subobject, the PKS is passed transparently from hop to hop, until it becomes the first subobject in the ERO. This occurs at the start of the CPS, which will usually be the domain boundary. The PKS MUST be preceded by an ERO subobject that identifies the LSR that must expand the PKS, so that the PKS is not encountered in ERO processing until the ERO is being processed by the LSR that is capable of correctly handling it.

An LSR that encounters a PKS when trying to identify the next hop retrieves the PCE-ID from the PKS and sends a Path Computation Request message to the PCE identified by the PCE-ID, containing the path-key object. Upon receiving it, the PCE identifies the computed path segment using the supplied path-key and returns the previously computed path segment in the form of explicit hops, using an ERO object contained in the Path Computation Reply to the requesting node. The requesting node inserts the explicit hops into the ERO and continues to process the TE LSP setup.

Retrieval of the explicit path associated with a PKS is no different from any other path computation request, except that the PCReq message MUST contain a PATH-KEY object and the Path-Key bit of the RP object MUST be set. If the receiving PCE does not recognize itself as the PCE named by the PCE ID, it MAY forward the PCReq to another PCE according to local policy; if it does not forward the request, it MUST respond with a PCRep containing a NO-PATH object. If the receiving PCE recognizes itself but cannot find the related CPS, or if policy does not allow the retrieval, it MUST send a PCRep containing a NO-PATH object, with a new bit number indicating that the PKS cannot be expanded. Upon receipt of a negative reply, the requesting LSR MUST fail the LSP setup and SHOULD use the procedures for loose hop expansion failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The token travels with the setup message until it reaches the router that has to expand it. That router sends a request to the PCE named in the token and asks for the real hops. The PCE looks up its stored segment and sends back the explicit route, which the router splices into the setup message. If the PCE cannot find the segment or will not release it, it refuses, and the router has to fail the setup.

sections.title: A Two-Autonomous-System Example
sections.content:
The RFC works through a simple two-AS topology with a PCE responsible for path computation in each AS. An LSP is requested from the ingress LSR in one AS to the egress LSR in the other. The ingress, acting as the PCC, sends a path computation request to PCE-1. PCE-1 is unable to compute an end-to-end path and invokes PCE-2. PCE-2 computes a path segment from ASBR-2 to the egress as {ASBR-2, C, D, Egress}. It could pass this path segment back to PCE-1 in full, or it could send back the path {ASBR-2, Egress} where the second hop is a loose hop.

To protect the confidentiality of the topology in the second AS while still specifying the path in full, PCE-2 may send PCE-1 a path segment expressed as {ASBR-2, PKS, Egress}, where the PKS is a Path-Key Subobject. In this case PCE-2 has identified the segment {ASBR-2, C, D, Egress} as a Confidential Path Segment. PCE-1 computes the path segment it is responsible for and supplies the full path to the PCC as {Ingress, A, B, ASBR-1, ASBR-2, PKS, Egress}. Signaling proceeds in the first AS as normal, but when the Path message reaches ASBR-2, the next hop is the PKS, and this must be expanded before signaling can progress further. ASBR-2 uses the information in the PKS to request PCE-2 for a path segment, and PCE-2 returns the segment {ASBR-2, C, D, Egress}, allowing signaling to continue to set up the LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: In the worked example, two networks each run their own path computation element. The second one works out its internal route, but hands back only a token in place of it. The first network assembles the whole route with the token in the middle and passes it along. When the setup message reaches the border router of the second network, that router asks its own path computation element to unlock the token, receives the real hops, and carries on.

sections.title: The Path-Key Subobject
sections.content:
Path-Keys are carried in PCReq and PCRep messages as part of the objects that carry path definitions, and in particular a Path-Key is carried in the Explicit Route Object on PCRep messages. In all cases the Path-Key is carried in a Path-Key Subobject (PKS).

The PKS is a fixed-length subobject containing a Path-Key and a PCE-ID. The Path-Key is an identifier, or token used to represent the CPS within the context of the PCE identified by the PCE-ID. The PCE-ID identifies the PCE that can decode the Path-Key, using an identifier that is unique within the domain that the PCE serves. It has to be mapped to a reachable IPv4 or IPv6 address of the PCE by the first node of the CPS, usually a domain border router, and a PCE MAY use one of its reachable IP addresses as its PCE-ID. Alternatively, and to provide greater security or increased confidentiality according to domain-local policy, the PCE MAY use some other identifier that is scoped only within the domain.

Two subobjects are defined so that both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses can be carried. The subobject type for the PKS with a 32-bit PCE ID is 64, and its length is always 8 bytes. The L bit SHOULD NOT be set, so that the subobject represents a strict hop in the explicit route. The subobject type for the PKS with a 128-bit PCE ID is 65, and its length is always 20 bytes. In both cases the PCE ID MUST be unique within the scope of the domain that the CPS crosses and MUST be understood by the LSR that will act as PCC for the expansion of the PKS.
sections.plainLanguage: The token is a small fixed-size record with two parts: the path-key itself, and an identifier for the path computation element that can decode it. Two shapes are defined, one for a 32-bit identifier and one for a 128-bit identifier, so that either an IPv4 or an IPv6 address can be used to name the decoder.

sections.title: Unlocking Path-Keys
sections.content:
When a network node needs to decode a Path-Key so that it can continue signaling for an LSP, it must send a PCReq to the designated PCE. The PCReq needs to be modified to support this usage, which differs from the normal path computation request. A new flag is defined to show that the PCReq relates to the expansion of a PKS, and a new object is defined to carry the PKS in the PCReq.

The new flag is the Path-Key bit, carried in the Request Parameters (RP) object. When set, the requesting PCC requires the retrieval of a Confidential Path Segment that corresponds to the PKS carried in a PATH-KEY object in the path computation request. The Path-Key bit MUST be cleared when the request is not related to a CPS retrieval.

The PATH-KEY Object has Object-Class 16 and Path-Key Object-Type 1. It MUST contain at least one Path-Key Subobject; the first PKS MUST be processed by the PCE and subsequent subobjects SHOULD be ignored. The format of the PCReq message is otherwise unchanged: the request is now either a segment computation or a path-key expansion, and the path-key expansion form carries only the PATH-KEY object. Thus the format of the message for use in normal path computation is unmodified.
sections.plainLanguage: To ask for the hidden route, a router sends the normal path computation request with one extra object in it and one extra flag set. The extra object carries the token to be expanded, and the flag says what the request is for. Ordinary path computation requests keep exactly the format they had before.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document describes tunneling confidential path information across an untrusted domain such as an AS, and there are many security considerations that apply to PCEP and RSVP-TE. The issues raised are the confidentiality of the CPS, meaning whether other network elements can probe for expansion of path-keys, possibly at random; the authenticity of the path-key, meaning resilience to alteration by intermediaries and to fake expansion of path-keys; and resilience from Denial-of-Service attacks, such as the insertion of spurious path-keys or the flooding of bogus path-key expansion requests.

Most of the interactions required by this extension are point to point and can be authenticated and made secure as described in RFC 5440 and RFC 3209. These are the PCC to PCE request, the PCE to PCE requests and responses, the PCE to PCC response, the LSR to LSR request and response, and the LSR to PCE request. A rogue LSR could modify the ERO and insert or modify Path-Keys, but that is an existing issue with RSVP and is not addressed here. The PCE can check that the LSR requesting the decode is the LSR at the head of the Path-Key, which largely contains the denial-of-service problem rather than a security issue, since a rogue LSR can issue random decode requests but these amount only to DoS.

Further protection comes from using a PCE ID that is only meaningful within the domain that contains the LSR at the head of the CPS. This may be an IP address that is only reachable from within the domain, or some value that is not an address at all. The former requires configuration of policy on the PCEs; the latter requires domain-wide policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things could go wrong: someone guessing tokens to unlock them, someone altering a token in flight, and someone flooding the PCE with requests to expand tokens that do not exist. Most of the traffic here is between two known neighbours and can be authenticated in the usual way. The PCE can also check that the request really came from the router that is supposed to expand the token, so random guessing only wastes the PCE's effort.

sections.title: Manageability Considerations
sections.content:
The treatment of a path segment as a CPS, and its substitution in a PCRep ERO with a PKS, is a function that MUST be under operator and policy control where a PCE supports it. The operator MUST be able to specify which path segments are to be replaced and under what circumstances. For example, an operator might set a policy that every path segment for its domain is replaced by a PKS when the request has been issued from outside the domain.

The operation of the PKS extensions requires that path-keys are retained by the issuing PCE for later retrieval, but the retrieval request may never be made, so a timer discards unwanted path-keys. The default value for this timer is the 10 minutes suggested in Section 2.1, and implementations SHOULD allow it to be overridden by operator configuration or policy. Once a path-key has been discarded, its value SHOULD NOT be immediately available for re-use for a new CPS, since this might lead to accidental misuse, and again the 30-minute default is recommended. Keeping the path-key and CPS after expansion may be valuable for debugging, but that SHOULD NOT be the default behaviour.

The configurable items MUST be added as readable objects in the existing PCEP MIB module and SHOULD be added as writable objects. A new MIB module MUST be created to allow inspection of path-keys, providing a mapping from path-key to path segment, the identity of the PCC that issued the original request, the request ID of that request, whether the path-key has been retrieved yet and by which PCC, and how long until the path segment and the path-key itself are discarded or become reusable.

The procedures extend PCEP but do not introduce new interactions between network entities, so no new liveness detection or monitoring is required, and no new tools for verifying correct operation are required. A PCE SHOULD maintain counters and logs of attempts to expand an unknown or expired path-key, duplicate attempts to expand the same path-key, and expiry of a path-key without an attempt to expand it. The only changes needed in the network are at head-end LSRs that build RSVP-TE Path messages containing PKSes and at the LSRs that discover such subobjects as next hops and must expand them. A PCE will not supply a PKS unless it knows the receiving LSR can handle it, so the only backward compatibility issue arises when a head-end LSR receives a PCRep with an ERO containing a PKS and does not know how to encode it into signaling; that legacy LSR must either fail the LSP setup or request a new path computation that avoids the domain which supplied the unknown subobject.
sections.plainLanguage: Whether a stretch of route is hidden is an operator decision, and the operator can set rules such as hiding everything in the local network when the request came from outside. The PCE keeps tokens for a limited time and then discards them, on a timer the operator can change. Management information records which tokens exist, which requests created them, and whether they have been used. Only two kinds of router need changes: the one that starts the setup and the one that expands the token.

fields.name: L bit and Type
fields.desc: The L bit SHOULD NOT be set, so the subobject represents a strict hop. The Type is 64 for a 32-bit PCE ID.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the subobject in bytes, including the Type and Length fields. Always 8.

fields.name: Path-Key
fields.desc: The identifier, or token, used to represent the Confidential Path Segment within the context of the PCE named by the PCE ID.

fields.name: PCE ID
fields.desc: A 32-bit identifier of the PCE that can decode this path-key, unique within the scope of the domain the CPS crosses.

viz.caption: The three security issues the RFC raises

items.title: Confidentiality of the CPS
items.text: Whether other network elements can probe for expansion of path-keys, possibly at random.

items.title: Authenticity of the path-key
items.text: Resilience to alteration by intermediaries, and to fake expansion of path-keys.

items.title: Denial-of-Service
items.text: Insertion of spurious path-keys, and flooding of bogus path-key expansion requests.
